Mining, energy & hydrogen · Namibia

Know what stands on and around your licence area before work starts

Namibian mining and petroleum law makes a licence holder get the owner’s written permission before working within 100 metres of a borehole, kraal, building or other structure, or within 300 metres of a surveyed erf. We give your land and community teams a dated, reviewed register of the structures in and around your licence area, measured to your planned workings, and show what changes over time. The same survey gives energy and green-hydrogen projects a land baseline before construction starts.

Send us your licence boundary The 100 m and 300 m rules

The problem, in your words

Large licence areas, and land that rarely stands still

Namibian licence areas are large and often remote, the land inside them is farmed, grazed and lived on, and the rules make the structures near your planned workings your problem before the first cut.

“What stands within 100 m of the pit?”

Before work starts near a borehole, a kraal, a building or any other structure, the owner’s written permission is needed. The first question is what stands there, and how far it is from the planned workings.

“The licence is bigger than we can walk.”

Exclusive prospecting licences and mining licences cover more ground than a land team can visit each season. New structures, tracks and cleared ground appear at the edges between visits.

“We can’t send a crew in there.”

Diamond restricted areas need the Minister’s permit to enter, and a drone flight in a national park needs approval. Satellite imagery covers them without anyone going in.

“We need the baseline before construction.”

Mines, bulk pipelines, transmission lines and roads all need an Environmental Clearance Certificate, and lenders ask what stood on the land before work began.

Who this is for

  • Land access and community relations teams
  • Exploration and licence managers
  • Environmental and rehabilitation teams
  • Project developers for solar, gas and green hydrogen
  • ESIA consultants and lender advisers
  • GIS and survey teams

The 100 m and 300 m rules

A register of what stands near your planned workings

A summary of the public rules as last reviewed on 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

The Minerals (Prospecting and Mining) Act 33 of 1992 bars a licence holder from exercising its rights on cultivated land, or “within a horizontal distance of 100 metres of any spring, well, borehole, reservoir, dam, dipping-tank, waterworks, perennial stream or pan, artificially constructed watercourse, kraal, building or any structure of whatever nature”, or within 300 m of a surveyed erf, “without the prior permission in writing of the owner” (s.52(1)(d)). The Petroleum (Exploration and Production) Act 2 of 1991 sets the same 100 m and 300 m distances for petroleum rights (s.16(1)(b)).

Both Acts also protect public land. Under the Minerals Act, work in towns and villages, on “a proclaimed road, including such parts adjoining such road as may… be regarded as the road reserve”, on aerodromes, harbours, railways and cemeteries, or on land reserved for public purposes needs the Minister’s prior permission (s.52(1)(b)); under the Petroleum Act it needs the Commissioner’s approval (s.16(1)(a)). On private land, the Minerals Act asks for a written compensation agreement with the owner, lodged with the Mining Commissioner, or an ancillary right (s.52(1)(a)).

What we deliver. We buffer the footprint of your planned workings, drill pads or plant by 100 m and 300 m, or by your own distances, and list each structure the review confirms inside each band: its ID, its distance to the workings, its coordinates and what the imagery shows, such as a dwelling, an outbuilding, a kraal or a dam. Your land team starts the permission conversation with a map instead of a guess.

What the imagery can show

Buildings, kraals, dams, reservoirs and cleared or cultivated ground usually show in the imagery. A borehole, a well, a spring or a dipping-tank is often too small to see from above. The register says which features it could confirm, and your field team’s points can be added to the same layers.

Licence edges and excavations

What changes inside your licence, and in a ring around it

For a mining licence, an exclusive prospecting licence or a petroleum licence, we map the structures, tracks and cleared ground inside the boundary and in a ring around it, and compare dated surveys to show what is new. Excavations, pits, spoil heaps and water-filled workings are mapped the same way, each with the first date it appears in the imagery. New tracks and access roads into the licence area are traced between dates.

Claims, the small-scale mining title, may be pegged only by Namibian citizens who hold a non-exclusive prospecting licence, or by companies whose shares only Namibian citizens may own (Minerals Act, s.25). A pit near your boundary may sit on a lawful claim. We map the ground and its changes; whether a working is authorised is for you and the Mining Commissioner to establish, and we never identify the people working there.

What you receive

  • Structures inside the licence and in a ring around it, with IDs, distances and coordinates
  • Excavations, pits, spoil and cleared ground, dated
  • New tracks and access roads between surveys
  • New and removed structures, with before-and-after views
  • A change notice after each scheduled survey

Uranium and open-pit mines

Construction, stockpiles and rehabilitation, dated

Uranium mining in the Erongo region, and quarries and mines elsewhere in the country, move a great deal of ground. We track it between dates:

  • Rehabilitation and revegetation on rehabilitated land and closed borrow pits, compared between dated scenes;
  • Construction and earthworks progress from dated drone orthophotos and elevation models, with maps of where ground has been cut or filled between visits;
  • Stockpile and earthworks volumes from drone elevation models, subject to the approvals and security clearances each flight requires;
  • Structures in the zones your engineers define, such as blast and exclusion zones, each listed with its distance to the zone edge.

If your survey team already flies the mine, send the orthophotos and elevation models and we run the same analysis on them.

Your own imagery

Drone orthophotos, elevation models and satellite GeoTIFFs you already hold go through the same structure, change and volume analysis, with a reviewer checking every result. Results depend on the imagery’s resolution and quality; we check a sample before we commit.

Mining work in other countries

Energy and green hydrogen

Dated baselines for onshore sites, routes and concessions

Namibia’s energy projects, from offshore discoveries with onshore supply bases to solar plants and green hydrogen in the south, all start with land: routes to agree, concessions to manage and a record of what stood there before construction. We provide:

  • A land-use and land-cover baseline of built-up land, cropland, bare ground, water and vegetation around the site, combined with the structure register;
  • An imagery history of the site and its routes from archived satellite scenes: what was built, cleared or changed, and roughly when;
  • Route option comparisons for the pipelines, water lines and transmission lines a new plant needs, counting the structures each alignment would affect;
  • Boundary, track and construction progress between dated surveys, with a notice after each one;
  • Host-town growth in towns such as Lüderitz, Walvis Bay and Oranjemund, from year-by-year settlement growth trends.

The southern green-hydrogen concessions lie inside Tsau ǁKhaeb National Park, where a drone flight needs approval and filming needs MEFT approval, so the baseline starts from satellite imagery.

Environmental clearance

The Environmental Management Act 7 of 2007 lists activities that need an Environmental Clearance Certificate from the Environmental Commissioner, among them “the transmission and supply of electricity”, mining and quarrying, “oil, water, gas and petrochemical and other bulk supply pipelines”, public roads, railways and harbours, and communication networks (GN 29 of 2012). We supply dated layers your ESIA consultant can use in the assessment and in monitoring.

For the Southern Corridor, a Strategic Environmental and Social Assessment for green energy production and industrialisation was put out for public comment until 4 September 2026 (Namibia Green Hydrogen Programme).

We found no statutory protection strip for pipelines in Namibia: send the widths your servitude agreements or standards use. A draft Downstream Gas Bill published by the Electricity Control Board in August 2026 is not law.

Land rights and project resettlement

A dated record of what stood in the footprint

In Namibia “resettlement” usually means the land-reform programme. Here we mean project land acquisition. We found no national law on project-induced resettlement: displacement runs through the sector Acts, the Expropriation Ordinance 13 of 1978 and the lender’s standard, such as the World Bank’s ESS5 or, on IFC- and Equator-financed projects, IFC Performance Standard 5.

On communal land, nobody may occupy or use land “other than under a right acquired in accordance with the provisions of this Act” (s.43), land may be withdrawn from a communal area only after the rights in it “have first been acquired by the State and just compensation for the acquisition of such rights is paid” (s.16), and a land board may grant occupational land rights for government and State-owned-enterprise projects (s.36A) (Communal Land Reform Act 5 of 2002). A Land Bill that would replace the communal and commercial land reform Acts is before Parliament; the current Acts still apply.

A cut-off-date baseline records the structures in your footprint on that date, with IDs, coordinates and imagery, and shows what has appeared since. It supports, and never replaces, your census, asset inventory and valuation. For a single disputed point, a location check puts the dated images of it on one sheet.

Diamond areas, parks and drones

Satellite first where access is restricted

Diamond restricted areas include onshore diamond mining licence areas, bulk-sampling areas, processing places and areas the Minister declares, and anyone who is not a listed official needs the Minister’s permit “to enter, reside, travel, work or be in, or to visit a restricted area” (Diamond Act 13 of 1999, ss.27(k), 52). In national parks, NCAA’s checklist allows no drone flight unless approval is granted.

In diamond restricted areas and national parks we work from satellite imagery unless your permits and consents cover a partner’s crew. Elsewhere, drone surveys are subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires: an NCAA Letter of Approval for each operation, the landowner’s permission, and the airfield rules near mine and lodge airstrips. Afridrone is working towards the approvals Namibia requires.

The Namibia drone-law guide

Restricted and prohibited areas, diamond areas and parks, the Letter of Approval and a 12-point checklist for anyone commissioning a drone survey, last reviewed on 27 September 2026.

How it works

From boundary file to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the licence or site boundary, the footprint of the planned workings or plant, and the distances and dates that matter. We agree the bands, the imagery and the deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Structures, excavations, tracks and cleared ground are mapped across the licence area from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or your own orthophotos.

  3. Check up close

    Your own flights, or drone surveys where approvals and permits allow, cover the areas that need more detail.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result, and the register, the change layers and the report go to the contacts you name.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, kraals, dams, excavations, tracks and cleared ground visible from the air
  • Measure them to your licence boundary and planned workings
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Record dated land baselines before construction

What we don’t do

  • Work offshore, or detect leaks, spills or slicks
  • Identify, count or follow people or vehicles
  • Decide whether a structure or a working is lawful, or who is entitled to compensation
  • Replace a census, a cadastral survey or a geological survey

Frequently asked questions

Which distances do you measure around planned workings?

The 100 m and 300 m distances in section 52 of the Minerals Act and section 16 of the Petroleum Act by default, measured from the footprint of the planned workings you send, plus any distance your own standards, your Environmental Clearance Certificate conditions or your lender use. Up to six distances can be reported in one survey.

Can you see boreholes, wells and springs?

Not reliably. Dams, reservoirs, kraals and buildings usually show in the imagery; a borehole, a well or a spring is often too small to see from above. The register says what the imagery could and could not show, and the points your field team collects can go into the same GIS layers.

Can you work inside a diamond restricted area or a national park?

From satellite imagery, yes, because nobody enters the area. Entering or being in a diamond restricted area needs the Minister’s permit under the Diamond Act, and a drone in a national park needs approval, so in those areas we work from satellite imagery unless your permits and consents cover a partner’s crew.

Who is digging at the edge of our licence?

We cannot say, and we do not try. We map excavations, pits, spoil and cleared ground, with the date each first appears. Small-scale claims can be pegged lawfully by Namibian citizens, so whether a working is authorised is for you and the Mining Commissioner to establish.

Do you work offshore, or detect spills?

No. We work onshore, on supply bases, laydown yards, pipeline and power-line routes, plant sites and the land around them. We do not detect leaks, spills or slicks.

Is this a resettlement census?

No. A dated register of the structures in a project footprint supports your census, asset inventory and valuation, and the cut-off-date records a lender’s standard asks for. The census, the consultations and the eligibility decisions stay with your team.

Send us your licence or site boundary

The boundary as KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile or GeoPackage, the footprint of the planned workings or plant, the distances that apply and the dates that matter. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
